title: Court investigates whether administration violated order over March 15 Alien Enemies Act deportation flights
description_short: Court investigates whether administration violated order over March 15 Alien Enemies Act deportation flights
description_medium: After deportation flights carrying Venezuelan nationals proceeded on March 15, 2025, Judge James Boasberg examined whether the administration had violated his direction to halt or return flights. He later found the administration had acted in bad faith and initiated contempt proceedings; the administration denied violating a valid order and appealed. The record should present the legal dispute and findings precisely rather than state uncontested defiance.
description_long: Deportation flights carrying Venezuelan nationals proceeded on March 15, 2025, after Judge James Boasberg directed the administration to halt or return flights. The ensuing dispute concerned whether officials had complied with that direction and whether the court had authority to issue it. Boasberg later found that the administration had acted in bad faith and initiated contempt proceedings. The administration denied violating a valid order and appealed. Those competing positions are part of the event, rather than reasons to erase the judge's finding or present the administration's defense as settled law. The episode illustrates a concrete conflict over judicial oversight of deportation operations: the court sought to determine what happened to the flights, while executive officials contested the legal basis for intervention. The supplied record supports describing the contempt inquiry and the findings it produced. It does not support treating all questions about the order's validity, compliance, or appellate outcome as finally resolved.

title: Capital One Reveals It Closed 300+ Trump Org Accounts Over Money Laundering Concerns
description_short: Capital One Reveals It Closed 300+ Trump Org Accounts Over Money Laundering Concerns
description_medium: Capital One disclosed for the first time in a court filing that it closed over 300 Trump Organization accounts in 2021 "for anti-money laundering reasons." Trump has maintained the closures were political "debanking." The Trump Organization sued Capital One in Florida federal court claiming "considerable financial harm." Capital One denies any political motivation, stating the closures followed months of internal compliance review triggered by AML flags.
description_long: Capital One said in a court filing that it closed more than 300 Trump Organization accounts in 2021 for anti-money-laundering reasons. Trump described the closures as politically motivated debanking, and the Trump Organization sued the bank in Florida federal court, alleging considerable financial harm. Capital One denied political motivation and said its decision followed months of compliance review prompted by anti-money-laundering concerns. The dispute concerns both access to banking services and competing explanations for a private institution's decisions. The bank's stated compliance rationale is not a criminal finding that the organization laundered money, just as Trump's allegation of political discrimination is not a court-established fact. Those distinctions are necessary to explain the filing without deciding the lawsuit through its competing claims. The supported account documents the number of affected accounts and the positions of the parties. It does not establish a final judgment on the closures' legality or quantify damages awarded.

title: SSA Inspector General Probes DOGE Employee Retaining 'God-Level' Data
description_short: SSA Inspector General Probes DOGE Employee Retaining 'God-Level' Data
description_medium: In March 2026, the Social Security Administration's Inspector General launched a formal investigation after a whistleblower alleged a former DOGE software engineer retained copies of two tightly restricted national databases — including the NUMIDENT containing records on nearly every American — on a thumb drive, and claimed 'God-level' access to SSA systems. The former employee allegedly planned to share the data with their new private-sector employer.
description_long: The Social Security Administration's inspector general opened an investigation in March 2026 after a whistleblower alleged that a former DOGE software engineer retained copies of two restricted databases on a thumb drive. One was NUMIDENT, described in the supplied account as containing records on nearly every American. The allegation also included a claim of unusually broad access to SSA systems and an intention to share the data with a new private-sector employer. The scale and sensitivity of the described databases make the incident relevant to oversight of government data access and retention. However, the event established by the supplied text is the opening of an investigation following those allegations. It does not establish that every asserted act was verified, that the employer received the data, or that a final misconduct finding had been issued. The explanation therefore attributes the retention and planned-sharing claims to the whistleblower and keeps the inspector general's inquiry distinct from its possible outcome.

The U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities occurred later and should not be presented as the trigger for this first retaliatory attack.

title: Trump Orders Expanded Presidential Supervision of Independent Executive Agencies
description_short: Trump Orders Expanded Presidential Supervision of Independent Executive Agencies

The order invoked Article II but also referred to an independent judiciary as a structural safeguard. The stored claim that Trump asserted complete authority over the courts or that Article II superseded judicial authority is unsupported.
description_long: Trump issued an executive order on February 18, 2025 asserting presidential supervision over the executive branch, including independent regulatory agencies. It required greater White House review of agencies' priorities and regulations and invoked Article II as the basis for that supervisory role. The action is relevant to the distribution of authority within the executive branch because agencies described as independent were brought within the order's review framework. title: Hegseth Plans to Cut Over 120 General and Admiral Positions 20 Percent of Top Leadership

title: January 2025 Immigration Executive Orders Do Not Suspend Habeas Corpus
description_short: January 2025 Immigration Executive Orders Do Not Suspend Habeas Corpus
description_medium: Trump's January 20, 2025 executive orders on immigration - including 'Protecting the American People Against Invasion' - direct enforcement of immigration laws and detention capabilities but do not suspend habeas corpus. The Alien Enemies Act was invoked later, in March 2025, in the Tren de Aragua deportation episode, and habeas corpus review remained available in federal courts. The card's claim of a day-one habeas suspension is unsupported.
description_long: Trump signed immigration orders on January 20, 2025, including Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The supplied correction describes directives on immigration enforcement and detention capacity, but identifies no provision suspending habeas corpus. Habeas review and the use of particular immigration authorities must therefore be kept distinct in this entry. The Alien Enemies Act was invoked later, in March 2025, in the deportation episode involving alleged Tren de Aragua members. That later action did not occur on inauguration day, and the correction notes that habeas review remained available in federal courts.
